summary: For ages 5–7: a fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a once-living thing, usually preserved in rock (often turned to stone) over a very long time; a palaeontologist is a scientist who finds and studies fossils to learn about dinosaurs and other ancient life. The target is recognition — say what a fossil is, identify examples (bone, tooth, footprint in rock), and name the scientist's job — plus two conceptual guards: a fossil is not the actual unchanged animal, and a trace like a footprint counts as a fossil too.
misconceptions: 'A fossil is the actual bone/animal, unchanged' — fossils are usually the original replaced by or turned to rock over a very long time.
'Only dinosaurs make fossils' — many living things (shells, plants, fish, footprints) become fossils.
'Palaeontologists study rocks in general / dig up dinosaurs that are still whole' — they study fossils and usually find scattered, incomplete remains.
'Fossils are found just lying around loose' — they are preserved IN rock and must be carefully found and freed.
'A footprint isn't a fossil because it isn't a body part' — preserved footprints (traces) are fossils too.

activities.title: Dig-site and museum: tap the clues
steps: Explore an illustrated dig-site and museum scene with several things to find and name.
Tap a knobbly shape half-buried in rock and read the caption: 'a bone, turned to stone, from a real animal that lived long ago'.
Tap a pointy tooth and a footprint pressed into rock; each reveals what it is and what it tells us about the animal.
Tap the person kneeling with a small brush and chisel to learn: 'a palaeontologist — a scientist who finds and studies fossils to figure out what dinosaurs were like'.
Follow a drill-down zoom that carries a fossil from the ground into a museum case, so you see where these clues end up.
Say in your own words what a fossil is and what a palaeontologist does.
activities.insight: Fossils are real clues preserved in rock (bones, teeth, and footprints all count), and there is a job that is all about finding and reading them.

activities.title: Fossil or not a fossil?
steps: Look at a short picture set: a fossil bone in rock, a plastic toy dinosaur, and a fresh leaf.
For each, decide 'fossil' or 'not a fossil' and say why.
Lift a flap to check the answer and read a short reason.
activities.insight: A fossil is a preserved remains or trace of something that was once alive, kept in rock over a very long time (often turned to stone) — not a toy and not a fresh, present-day thing.

activities.title: Brush away the rock: uncover and sort a dig (optional motivating vehicle)
steps: Brush or scrape away virtual rock to reveal a hidden fossil.
Drag each find — a bone, a tooth, a footprint — to a labelled tray.
Read the name of each find as you sort it.
activities.insight: Finding, freeing and sorting fossils is part of what a palaeontologist does — fossils are often carefully freed from rock rather than simply picked up.

activities.title: Footprint puzzle: is it a fossil, and whose foot is it? (check of understanding)
steps: Consider: someone finds a dinosaur footprint turned to stone. Is that a fossil, even though it isn't a bone?
Then decide: is the stony footprint the dinosaur's actual foot that got hard, or is it something else? Explain.

Try the follow-ups: if the dinosaur's foot isn't in the stone, how can the stone still show its shape? Name two other things besides a footprint that could become a fossil. What do we call a scientist who studies fossils?
activities.insight: A fossil is any remains OR trace of a long-ago living thing preserved in rock, so footprints count; the stony footprint is not the foot itself — the dinosaur pressed its foot into soft mud and walked on, and over a very long time the mud holding the print hardened into rock, keeping the shape.

checkQuestion: Someone finds a dinosaur footprint turned to stone. Is that a fossil, even though it isn't a bone? And is the stony footprint the dinosaur's actual foot that got hard, or is it something else? Explain.
checkAnswer: Yes, it's a fossil — a fossil is any remains or trace of a long-ago living thing preserved in rock, so footprints count as well as bones and teeth. It is NOT the actual foot: the real foot is long gone. The dinosaur pressed its foot into soft mud, and over a very long time that print filled in and hardened to rock, keeping the shape. Scientists who study fossils are called palaeontologists.
